Frequently asked questions

How to read the liquidation levels chart, what the lines, bubbles and panels mean, and where the data comes from.

What is a liquidation levels chart?

Futures are traded with leverage. When price moves far enough against a position, the exchange closes it by force and the position is liquidated. The price that triggers this is the liquidation price, and where many positions share nearly the same liquidation price you get a liquidation level.

The chart records these prices candle by candle. A batch of positions opened on a given candle draws a horizontal line from that candle, running right until price touches it. Lines above price are short liquidations, lines below are long liquidations, and the brighter the line, the more positions are estimated to be liquidated there.

Traders watch it because liquidations turn into market orders. Once price runs into a dense cluster, forced closes speed the move up, and stops sitting just inside the cluster tend to fill at the worst price. The levels are estimated from open interest and common leverage settings; they are not resting orders.

For example: BTC trades at 82,500 and the lines between 80,300 and 80,600 below are dense and bright. A wick drops to 80,250, those longs are liquidated into market sells and the drop accelerates. Once the wick recovers, all of those lines end at its tip, because that batch of liquidations has already happened.

Reading the chart
What do the lines on a liquidation levels chart mean?

Each line is the estimated liquidation price of a batch of positions. It starts at the candle where those positions were opened and runs right until price touches it; at that point the positions count as liquidated and the line ends. Lines above price are short liquidations, lines below are long liquidations.

A brighter line means a larger estimated liquidation size. Only lines that are still running right, untouched, are live levels now.

FAQ

How to read a footprint chart, what the markers and signals mean, and where the data comes from.

What is a footprint chart?

A regular candle gives you four prices and one volume number: whether the last 15 minutes closed up or down, and how much traded. It can't tell you who was buying, who was selling, or which price traded the most.

A footprint chart (also called an order flow chart or bid/ask footprint) slices each candle into price levels and prints two numbers at every level: on the left, the volume sold aggressively at that price; on the right, the volume bought aggressively. Futures traders have long used it for order flow analysis, and it reads the same way on BTC, ETH and other crypto perps and spot pairs.

Aggressive means the taker side of a trade. A market buy that lifts the offer is a taker buy; a market sell that hits the bid is a taker sell. Makers, whose limit orders rest on the book waiting to be filled, don't count. Price moves because someone is willing to pay the spread to get filled right now.

Say a strong green candle closes near its high. Break it open and the top few levels show almost no taker buying, while most of the volume sits in the lower half of the bar. Nobody chased the last leg up; it was probably shorts getting stopped out, and the move may not have much left. A plain candle can't tell you that.

Reading the chart
How do you read the numbers on a footprint chart?

Each level reads Bid × Ask. The left number is volume that traded at the bid, meaning taker sells; the right number is volume that traded at the ask, meaning taker buys.

The "Coin / USD" toggle in the toolbar switches units. When cells get narrow, numbers are shortened to 52, 5.2, .45 or 1.2K. Narrower still, each cell shows a single number: bid and ask combined (in Avg size mode, the average trade size of both sides). Hover a cell to see the exact figure.
